newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ capital's businesses want quick end to talks.
newsitem.headline: NZ capital's businesses want quick end to talks.

text.p: Politicians need to sort out urgently a coalition government to restore confidence to the Wellington economy, region mayors and business leaders said on Thursday.
They said political procrastination was delaying investment and spending, and causing uncertainty at local government level, NZPA reported.
"My call is for (NZ First leader) Winston Peters and the other parties to get their act together, stop the games and get on with coalition," Kapiti Mayor Brett Ambler said.
He believed Kapiti was suffering from a state of flux and indecision.

Nationalist NZ First holds the balance of power after the October 12 election and is negotiating with both the conservative National party and the main opposition Labour party over the shape of the next government.
Peters indicated on Wednesday the timetable for talks could be extended.
Wellington Chamber of Commerce chief executive Ray Harding said businesses were noticing a drop-off in trade. The chamber was surveying members to determine the effects of the delay.
Harding said business volumes must decline as government departments held off spending. The trickle-down effect would be significant.
Manufacturers Federation chief executive Simon Arnold said political uncertainty was forcing business to delay investment decisions.
Upper Hutt Mayor Rex Kirton said some investment in retail and industrial sectors spoken of just before the election had not materialised because of the uncertainty.
Porirua Mayor John Burke said he was prepared to wait for a conclusion while Wellington Mayor Mark Blumsky acknowledged business was slow but said he did not know why.
Some business leaders dispute whether business is affected by the uncertainty.

Wellington Regional Council chairman Stuart Macaskill, Steel and Tube chief executive Nick Calavrias, and Hutt Valley Chamber of Commerce and Industry executive director Michael Romanos did not believe business had been affected by political uncertaity.
